---
title: "Hardy–Littlewood Maximal Function and the Maximal Theorem"
---

In what follows, we will denote $B(x,r)$ the open ball centered at $x$ with radius $r$. 

::: {#r-13-1 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### Definition 13.1 — Locally integrable

A function $f:\mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R$ is said to be locally integrable, or in $L_\mathrm{loc}^1$, if $f$ is integrable with respect to Lebesgue measure when restricted to any compact set. (or equivalently, if for every $x$ there is an $r > 0$ such that $f$ is integrable on $B(x,r)$ wrt to Lebesgue measure.)
:::

For $f\in L_\mathrm{loc}^1$, $x\in \mathbb R^n$, and $r > 0$ we define $$A_r f(x) = \frac{1}{m(B(x,r))} \int_{B(x,r)} f(y) dm(y)$$which is simply the average of $f$ over the ball around $x$ with radius $r$. This can be seen interpreted as the mean value of $f$ over the ball centered around $x$ with radius $r$. 

Some additional remarks:

1. If $f$ is continuous at $x$, it is easy to see that $$\lim_{r\rightarrow 0} A_r f(x) = f(x)$$
2. This cannot occur for all $f$ since if we modify it at a single point, it would fail there. Take for example $\tilde f(x) =1$ but $\tilde f(y) = 0, y \neq x$, then the limit becomes $0$ as $r\rightarrow 0$ whereas the LHS is $1$.

::: {#r-13-2 .callout-note .definition-box}

#### Definition 13.2 — Hardy-Littlewood Maximal function

If $f\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb R^n)$, then the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function $Hf$ is defined by $$Hf(x) := \sup_{r> 0} A_r|f|(x)$$
:::

::: {#fig-viz-maximalfunction-1}

        el("path", { d: fPath, fill: "none", stroke: ACCENT, strokeWidth: 2 }),

        el("path", { d: rPath, fill: "none", stroke: RED, strokeWidth: 2 }),
        el("circle", { cx: sr(r0), cy: sy(a0), r: 4, fill: RED }),

        lab(R2, Math.max(T + 12, sy(h0) - 6), "Hf(x) = sup", BLUE, "end"),
        lab(R2, T + 12 > sy(h0) - 24 ? sy(h0) + 18 : T + 12, "r ↦ Aᵣ|f|(x)", RED, "end")
      )
    );
  }
  var el = document.getElementById('viz-maximalfunction-1');
  if (el) ReactDOM.createRoot(el).render(React.createElement(MaximalFunction));
})();
</script>

Interactive: the averages $A_r|f|(x)$ over the window $[x-r,x+r]$ (red), and the maximal function $Hf(x) = \sup_{r>0} A_r|f|(x)$ (blue). The right panel plots $r \mapsto A_r|f|(x)$; its supremum is $Hf(x)$.
:::

This functions essentially computes the average over the absolute value of $f$ over all radii, and picks the largest such average amongst those radii. It is therefore a "measure" of the local average of $|f|$.

One can verify that $Hf$ is a measurable function by noting  $$(Hf)^{-1}(\alpha, \infty) =\bigcup_{r>0} (A_r|f|)^{-1}\{(\alpha, \infty)\}$$where $A_rf$ is a continuous function for $f\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}$, and thus we have preimages of open sets under continuous functions which are still continuous, and thus a union of open sets. 

::: {#r-13-3 .callout-important .theorem-box}

#### Theorem 13.3 — (Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Theorem)

If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$, then $\forall \alpha > 0$ we have $$m(\{x: Hf(x) > \alpha\}) \leq \frac{3^n}{\alpha} \int |f|dm(x)$$

::: {.callout-note .proof-box collapse="true"}

#### Proof

Let $E_\alpha = \{x: Hf(x) > \alpha\}$.  For each $x\in E_\alpha$ there exists $r_x > 0$ so that $$A_{r_x}|f|(x) > \alpha$$ by the definition of the supremum. With this, we can for each $x$ have an associated open ball, and we may denote this collection of open balls as $\mathcal C$. Given $c < m(\bigcup_{x\in E_a} B(r, r_x))$, we can use the covering lemma from [Lecture 12](lecture-12.qmd) to find $x_1, ..., x_k$ in $E_\alpha$ so that $k$ balls $\{B(x_i, r_{x_i})\}$ are disjoint and $$\frac{c}{3^n} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k m(B(x_i, r_{x_i}))$$
However, by our choice of $r_x$'s, i.e. $A_{r_{x_i}}|f|(x_i) > \alpha$, we have $$\frac{c}{3^n} \leq \sum_{i=1}^k m(B(x_i, r_{x_i})) \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{\alpha}\int_{B(x_i, r_{x_i})} |f|(x) dm(x) \leq \frac{1}{\alpha} \int |f|(x) dm(x)$$where the last inequality follows from the disjointness of the balls. Since this holds $\forall c < m(E_\alpha)$, we also have $$m(E_\alpha) \leq \frac{3^n}{\alpha} \int |f|dm$$
as desired. $\square$
:::
:::
